new_findings_today.title: A large, previously-unreported burst of production errors hit nakshiq.com on 2026-09-20 -- a 300-second platform timeout cluster spanning ~35 route types (lifetime count 448, 370 users) plus dozens of transient Supabase getMonthData/getDestination connection failures concentrated between roughly 08:24 and 12:40 UTC that day -- currently quiet (0 errors in the last 6 hours) but materially different from the 'clean' picture every recent weekly QA report has described
new_findings_today.detail: Vercel's get_runtime_errors tool, queried with since=24h, returned 50 distinct error groups -- a much larger and more varied set than any prior week's pull (09-14 reported only 2 small pre-existing clusters over a 7-day window). The two dominant signals: (1) 'Vercel Runtime Timeout Error: Task timed out after 300 seconds', lifetime count=448, users=370, first-seen 2026-07-02, last-seen 2026-09-20T12:34:13Z, spanning roughly 35 distinct route patterns including destination/month/cost pages, blog, treks, with-kids, family, several vs/ comparison pages, and multiple cron endpoints (audit-cache-headers, alerts, audit-supabase-advisors, canary-probe); and (2) roughly 45 distinct 'Supabase getMonthData(<destination>,<month>) failed: undefined undefined' and 'Supabase getDestination(<destination>) failed after 3 attempts: undefined undefined' error groups (4-13 occurrences each), almost all clustered in a burst on 2026-09-20 between about 08:24 and 12:40 UTC, plus one distinct 'PGRST002 Could not query the database for the schema cache. Retrying.' occurrence in the same window. Narrowing the query to since=6h and since=1h both returned zero errors of any kind, meaning nothing has recurred in the roughly 14-18 hours before this QA session started. Direct live re-probes just now of 5 of the specific pages named in the error groups (jodhpur/february, tungnath/may, halebidu, gandikota, kumbhalgarh) all returned HTTP 200 with correct, real content. Read together: this looks like a real but currently-resolved burst of Supabase-side connectivity failures (the 'undefined undefined' error shape suggests a network/connection-level failure rather than a data-specific bug, since it hit dozens of unrelated destinations with the same shape) coinciding with a period of platform-level task timeouts, rather than an ongoing outage -- but the scale (448 lifetime timeout occurrences, 370 affected users) and the breadth of routes affected is large enough that it should not be waved off as routine. The 'first=2026-07-02' timestamp on the timeout cluster also raises the question of whether this class of error has been present and simply not surfaced by prior weeks' narrower checks (which specifically searched for a Postgres '57014' statement-timeout signature and did not find one, correctly, since this is a different error string).

new_findings_today.title: The Business Report's shared 'By the numbers' table (sectionResults() in build_report.js) still renders developer jargon (TTFB, hreflang, 2xx/5xx, SW, p90, raw millisecond figures) to the business-owner persona, even after the 09-03 fix for the same class of leak (NEW-2026-08-14-005)
new_findings_today.detail: Scanning today's freshly-generated NakshIQ_Business_Report.docx text (per the skill's own verification recipe) found two leaks. (1) run.executor -- rendered verbatim as a header line on all three personas -- named 'qa/SKILL.md' and 'Supabase/Vercel' in its text; this session rewrote run.executor in plain language for today's report and it now scans clean. (2) A second, separate leak that this session did NOT modify the code for: buildBusiness() in qa/_lib/build_report.js calls the same sectionResults(m) helper used by the QA persona to render a 'By the numbers (today's measured results)' table, and that helper's output includes strings like 'TTFB min 188/median 2845/max 3658 ms', 'hreflang en/hi/x-default 14/14/14', '20/21 2xx', and 'SW nakshiq-v60' -- all genuine developer jargon a business owner would not recognize, even though none of it is a file path, commit hash, or NEW-2026- style ID (the specific things the 09-03 fix targeted and the skill's scan recipe checks for). The function's own code comment says it 'is kept because it is already human-language with no technical references', which today's scan shows is not accurate.
new_findings_today.evidence: unzip -p NakshIQ_Business_Report.docx word/document.xml | python3 -c "...strip tags..." on this session's first draft (before the run.executor fix) showed 'qa/SKILL.md' and 'Supabase/Vercel' in the header line; after the fix, that specific leak is gone. The same scan, run again after the fix, still shows the sectionResults() table text verbatim: 'B — Destination availability + TTFB PASS 10/10 → 200; TTFB min 188/median 2845/max 3658 ms', 'D — SEO meta PASS stutter 0; canonical 14/14; hreflang en/hi/x-default 14/14/14; og:image 14/14', 'I — Core routes PASS 20/21 2xx; TTFB min 171/median 1047/p90 undefined/max 2288 ms', 'G — PWA / SW / manifest PASS SW nakshiq-v60; icons 3; shortcuts 5'.
new_findings_today.recommendation: Add a separate, plain-language section-results renderer for the business persona only (e.g. 'Destination pages loaded correctly, though a bit slower than usual right after this week's update' instead of raw TTFB ms figures), leaving sectionResults() as-is for the QA persona where the detail is appropriate. This is a smaller, different leak than NEW-2026-08-14-005 (jargon rather than file paths/commit hashes), so it wasn't caught by that fix's scan criteria -- worth widening the scan recipe itself to also flag common technical abbreviations (TTFB, SW, p90, 2xx/4xx/5xx, hreflang) going forward, not just file extensions and hex tokens.

business_summary.headline: Today's check found the website itself in good shape — 10 spot-checked destination pages, the emergency-contact information, the search index, and every core page all came back clean, even after a fresh update went out to the site this past week. The one thing that needs real attention: while digging into the site's error records to make sure nothing broke unnoticed, this check found a sizeable burst of technical errors that happened yesterday (September 20th) for a few hours — pages briefly failing to load their data for dozens of destinations, plus a much larger, longer-running pattern of pages timing out that goes back to early July. Both appear to have quieted down — nothing has recurred in the last several hours, and every affected page loads correctly right now — but the scale of it is bigger than anything reported in recent weeks and deserves a developer's attention rather than being assumed fixed just because it's quiet.
context: This is one in a running series of automated, scheduled health checks of nakshiq.com that has been going since early May 2026 — every check in this report was performed live against the real site today, not estimated or carried over from a prior day.

This check's own schedule is confirmed to be weekly (Mondays), not daily as its name suggests — that mismatch was found last week and hasn't been corrected yet, but this week's check is exactly on schedule, so there is no new gap in coverage.
A new version of the website went live sometime in the past week. Every check performed on it today came back healthy.

This week's check also went a step further than usual on one point: instead of relying on a quick stand-in check for the site's error history, it looked across several different time windows (a full day, then narrower 6-hour and 1-hour slices) specifically to make sure a newly-found issue wasn't still actively happening. That extra step is what turned up the technical-error burst described below, and also what confirms it has genuinely quieted down rather than just going unmeasured.

business_about_this_report.note: How this report gets made, for context:
items: This check normally runs on a schedule without anyone needing to trigger it by hand — it's currently set to run weekly rather than daily, a known issue still awaiting a decision. It visits the live site the same way a real visitor would — loading pages, following links, and reading what actually comes back — rather than just checking that the underlying code looks correct.

Every number in this report comes from something measured today: a page that was actually loaded, a database query that was actually run, or a screen that was actually looked at. Nothing here is estimated or copied forward from a previous day without being re-checked.

Three versions of this report are produced from the same underlying checks: this plain-language version for a business owner, a more detailed version for whoever is doing QA review, and a fully technical version for whoever is fixing things day-to-day.
When something can't be checked for a good reason, that's stated plainly rather than skipped silently or guessed at.
If a number in this report looks surprising, the more detailed companion reports break every section down further, with the specific evidence behind each pass or fail.
